rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Yāsīn shares the preceding two sūrahs’ central concerns, while treating some earlier topics with historical and human nature arguments.
rows.anchor: the central theme of this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah begins with prophethood, continuing the topic that closed the preceding sūrah.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an affirmation of prophethood – the topic on which the previous sūrah ended.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the preceding sūrahs, this one is founded on gratitude and its implications.
rows.anchor: like the previous sūrahs it is based on gratitude and what it entails.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–12 establish Muhammad’s prophethood: the wise Qur’an is the strongest evidence that he is God’s messenger calling people to the straight path.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān replete with wisdom is the greatest evidence to the fact that he is a messenger of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is God’s favor to people who lacked divine guidance and wandered astray; arrogance makes them deny it, while inherited traditions and future desires block reflection.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān is a great favour from the Almighty and powerful God to people who till then were deprived of any divine guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not worry over those who will not listen; he should promise a great reward to those who fear God and are ready to receive counsel.
rows.anchor: He should give glad tidings of a great reward to those who fear God and are prepared to listen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should leave nonlisteners to God, who has recorded their deeds and can deal with them.
rows.anchor: He should leave the matter of those who do not listen to God. He has recorded all their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt pairs with Yāsīn and shares its main themes, though its argument and discourse sequence differ.
rows.anchor: This sūrah forms a pair with Sūrah Yāsīn, the previous sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism remains the group’s central concern, with this sūrah especially refuting the divinity attributed to angels.
rows.anchor: a specific aspect of monotheism – refutation of divinity imputed to angels – is taken up in detail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Judgment scenes emphasize the conflict between the masses and their idolatrous leaders.
rows.anchor: the mutual row between the masses and the leaders of the Idolaters is highlighted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic histories show that God destroyed nations that rejected their messengers, while the messengers and their followers alone succeeded.
rows.anchor: nations which denied their messengers were destroyed by the Almighty; only the messengers and their followers were successful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels obey God and praise Him; their conduct testifies that they are servants, not associates, despite what foolish people suppose.
rows.anchor: Through their very deeds, they bear witness that they are very obedient to God and are not His associates

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only angels approach God; jinn and devils cannot reach the High Realm, and attempts to overhear its secrets are repelled by angels and pursued by shooting stars.
rows.anchor: The jinn and devils do not have access to the High Realm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The portrayal of the mockers’ Judgment fate reassures the Prophet: their followers will curse leaders for blocking them from following him.
rows.anchor: their masses will curse their leaders for stopping them from following the Prophet of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders will answer that followers themselves are to blame for rejecting truth after it became clear.
rows.anchor: leaders will rebuke their followers that they themselves are to blame for denying the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 40–61 describe the reward and eternal bliss of believers who backed God’s messenger despite pressure from companions and leaders.
rows.anchor: A description of the reward of the believers who in spite of the efforts of their companions and leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 62–70 allude to the fate of people who blindly followed their forefathers in opposing a messenger and his practice.
rows.anchor: The fate of those who in their frenzy of blindly followed their forefathers opposed a messenger of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 71–148 provide historical evidence that warned nations rejecting their messengers were destroyed, while the followers survived; God’s blessing and mercy belong to messengers and their followers.
rows.anchor: nations which denied their respective messengers after these messengers had warned them were destroyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion returns coherently to the opening: through Gabriel, the angels testify that they obey God, praise Him, and are His servants rather than partners.
rows.anchor: In this concluding section, the discourse coherently returns to the opening topic of the sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God assures Muhammad that His help and dominance over the opponents are reserved for him and his followers; the opponents will lose because jealousy and arrogance turned them against the messenger they had awaited.
rows.anchor: God’s help and dominance over his opponents are reserved for him and his followers; these opponents are destined to lose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad should ignore the opponents and continue his work with restraint; success belongs to God’s messengers alone.
rows.anchor: He should ignore them and keep doing his job while exercising restraint. Success is destined for the messengers of God alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle wāw marks an oath; Qur’anic oaths substantiate a claim rather than venerate the object sworn by, following al-Farāhī’s treatment in al-Im‘ān fī Aqsām al-Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: The oaths sworn by the Almighty in the Qur’ān are not meant to venerate the object by which the oaths are sworn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farāhī treated the purpose of Qur’anic oaths at length in al-Im‘ān fī Aqsām al-Qur’ān, which Islahi says he translated into Urdu.
rows.anchor: My mentor Imām H@amīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī has dealt in detail on this issue in his book al-Im‘ān fī Aqsām al-Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “those arrayed in ranks” describes angels, as Gabriel’s later words about angels standing arrayed confirm.
rows.anchor: The word ِاتَّافَّالص occurs here as an attribute of the angels, and this is evident from a succeeding verse of this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels in view belong to the High Realm and stand arrayed around God’s throne; Sūrah al-Zumar similarly describes angels encircling the throne in praise.
rows.anchor: those angels are referred to here that belong to the High Realm and stand arrayed in ranks around the throne of the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zajr means to scold or drive someone away; here it describes angels repelling devils who try to enter the High Realm, a process detailed in the following verses.
rows.anchor: The word زجر means “to scold and drive away someone”. It refers to another attribute of these angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels’ third attribute is praising and extolling God, as in the cited descriptions of angels in Sūrah al-Zumar and this sūrah.
rows.anchor: In other words, the angels praise and extol the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects as linguistically incorrect the view that the three coordinated attributes belong to different beings.
rows.anchor: the opinion of those who have regarded these attributes to belong to different entities is, in my opinion, linguistically incorrect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coordinated attributes all belong to angels and unfold in sequence: arraying before God, repelling Satan, then praising God, like the sequence in prayer.
rows.anchor: there occurs a gradual sequence in these attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your God is One” completes the oath: the angels’ worship and praise witness to God’s oneness.
rows.anchor: This verse forms the complement of oath ( muqsam ‘alayh). After presenting this worship and praising and extolling of the angels as witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who make angels God’s daughters or partners and worship them for intercession are foolish; the angels’ own worship contradicts them.
rows.anchor: extremely foolish are those who have made angels associates of God by regarding them as His daughters and are worshipping them hoping to receive their intercession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second statement says God alone rules the heavens, earth, what lies between, and all the east and west; He directly administers every part of the universe without partners or need of help.
rows.anchor: He alone is the master of every nook and corner of His universe and directly administers them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels have no delegated partnership in cosmic administration; they are obedient ambassadors and workers who carry out God’s directives.
rows.anchor: they are His obedient ambassadors and workers. Whatever they do is in compliance with the directives of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “mashāriq” conveys the vastness of the east; Qur’anic plurals can convey magnitude, while dual forms can indicate the two sides, as in “the two easts” and “the two wests.”
rows.anchor: at times plurals of a word indicate their vastness and enormity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Lord of the west” is elided after “Lord of the east” because the west is understood as subsumed under the primary east; the Qur’an sometimes states both explicitly.
rows.anchor: There is a suppression of the words بَر َمْالْبِارَغ after بَر ِقِارَشَمْال on account of contextual indications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The east may be singled out because polytheists especially worshipped the sun, which rises in the east.
rows.anchor: polytheists have worshipped the sun the most and the sun rises from the east.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stars adorn the lowest heaven and guard it from rebellious devils. Polytheists mistakenly thought devils could access the High Realm and sought them for knowledge of the unseen, but no one can enter it and jinn are struck by meteors.
rows.anchor: The fact of the matter is that no one has access to the High Realm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥifẓan is an emphatic verbal noun from an omitted verb, with the implied construction “We protected it protection.”
rows.anchor: The word اًظْفِح is a verbal noun of a suppressed verb meant to emphasize it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stars both embellish the lowest heaven and serve as projectiles against devils, a subject also described in Qur’an 67:5 and 15:16–18.
rows.anchor: on the one hand stars are an embellishment for the lowest heaven and on the other these very stars are used by the Almighty to check the devils

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negation denies the intended result: devils attempt to overhear the High Realm but cannot, and are pelted from every side.
rows.anchor: The negation of the verb in َلَا َونُعَّمَّسَی is meant to negate the purpose of the verb.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duḥūran means driving away or repulsing, and wāṣib means eternal; devils are repelled in this world and face everlasting punishment in the next.
rows.anchor: The word اًورُحُد means “to drive away” and “to repulse”, and the word بٌ ِاصَو means “eternal”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God’s secure defenses, devils cannot reach the High Realm or its secrets; one may snatch something only briefly before a bright star pursues him from the heavenly forts.
rows.anchor: there is no chance that they have access to the High Realm or its secrets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account establishes that angels are not divine partners and devils have no access to heavenly secrets, so worshipping angels as God’s daughters is foolish.
rows.anchor: neither are angels partners of God in any sense nor do devils have any access to the High Realm
